Three audiences

Opener beat: "Who's pitched someone this month without calling it a pitch?" Take a few hands. Investment, advice, a board seat, intros, word of mouth, a key hire. It's all pitching.

Your point: investors buy the narrative, customers buy the facts. Same business, different lead.

Match the detail to what they already know. Someone who knows your space wants your edge. Someone who doesn't needs the problem first.

Part 3 · What makes a good pitch

Start with the Problem

1
What problem do you solve?
2
Who has it?
3
What does it cost them today?
4
Who will pay to make it go away?
Lead the conversation

If you don't clearly describe your business, a VC will disengage or, worse yet, start making up their vision of what you should be doing!

Fitler MBA · S11 · Part 3

Start with the problem

Beat: everyone writes their own four answers. Three minutes. Walk the room.

"Who will pay" is the one founders skip. Having the problem and paying to fix it are different things.

Tell it as a story. One customer, the moment it hurt, what it cost. Éclat version: an office manager in late November with 200 client gifts to send and nothing ordered.

The Sequoia pitch structure

Story slot: where you've used Sequoia's structure.

The reveal: "You already wrote slide 1. It's your elevator pitch."

Traction is "progress to date." The Ask: every pitch ends with one. Both are ours, not Sequoia's. That's why they're tinted.

Services: "Product" means how an engagement works, step by step.

A checklist, not a script. Put your strongest section first. Order changes with stage: no traction yet, lead with you and the problem. Traction, lead with the proof. Market never drops out.

Predict before the click: "Which test does each section help pass?" Let them call a few. One click fills in all the dots.

Team: your view from the VC side. A great team can pivot to find the fit. A weak team fails even with a good product.

Part 4 · Sizing the market

TAM / SAM / SOM: The Slide Everyone Hates!

TAM
Total Addressable Market
Potential customers × average annual revenue per customer
SAM
Serviceable Available Market
TAM × % you can realistically serve
SOM
Serviceable Obtainable Market
SAM × % you can realistically capture
The investor's read

Prove to the investors you know the market inside and out.

Formulas adapted from Seer Interactive's market sizing guide

TAM / SAM / SOM

Predict first: "What's wrong with '1% of a $50B market'?" Let the room take it apart before you say anything.

Your experience: most market slides don't hold up. You've seen hundreds. (Keep the 95% spoken, not printed.)

Walk the formulas top to bottom. Each one narrows the one above it. The SOM line is the one that matters: what you can realistically capture.

Three common failures: TAM borrowed from an analyst report. SAM never defined. SOM is "we only need 1%."

TAM tells an investor if it's worth their time. SOM tells them if you know your business.

Top-down claims a share of a big number. Bottom-up counts actual customers. Investors trust bottom-up and use top-down as a sanity check.

Callback: this is the S09 smallest-viable-market test, with numbers.

All figures are illustrative assumptions for teaching. They are not Éclat's numbers. Avg order assumed 100 boxes × $25.

Bottom-up SOM

The numbers start pre-filled. Every one is an assumption. The room changes two: conversion and December capacity. Click the − / + buttons (they don't advance the slide). Watch which gate lights up.

Predict: "If one in ten tastings becomes an order, what does a customer cost?" $150 a tasting × 10 = $1,500. That's CAC.

Predict: "Which gate binds for Éclat in December?" Production. Holiday gifting piles into six weeks. The rest of the year, demand binds. SOM changes by season.

Try live: conversion to 1 in 20 → CAC Budget binds (8). Capacity up to 3,000 → sales channel or CAC budget takes over.

Sales channel capacity is limited by time. CAC budget is limited by money. A founder doing all the selling hits the channel wall.

S09 callback: CAC budget says how many you can buy. LTV says whether you should. A company that orders every December is a recurring customer with a high LTV, so it can carry a high CAC.

Services: CAC includes the owner's unpaid time. Proposals, coffees, pitches that don't close. Count it.

Which gate binds: software, usually demand or sales channel. Services, usually production. Ten consultants can only bill so many hours. Physical products, it moves around.

The line for this room: "Your market isn't your limit. Your team is."

SOM is where the pro forma revenue line starts.

Fitler MBA · S11 · Part 5

Where does the round get the company?

Open with the callback: "Which tests had the fewest slides behind them?" 6 and 7. Both ride on The Ask.

Start with the outcome, not the number. Milestones are what make you fundable next time, or profitable.

Walk the four gates, same names as the last slide. The classic mistake: asking for marketing money when production is the gate. You pay to create demand you can't fill. Investors catch it.

CAC budget: money buys customers, but only if LTV beats CAC. Otherwise you're raising money to buy losses.

Demand-limited is the hard one. Money doesn't fix an offer nobody wants.

1 · The gate

Production Level

  • Goal: 30 next holiday season

Equipment$40K

What kind of money fits?

An equipment loan, a seasonal line of credit, or a revenue share. Not VC. Same pitch skills, different deal.

Illustrative assumptions for teaching. Not Éclat's numbers or plans.

Éclat's ask

Run it left to right: the gate from slide 13, the milestones that lift it, then the money that pays for the milestones. The amount follows. Never the other way.

Sizing the raise: cost to hit the milestones plus a buffer. Use of funds is just this list. What the investor gets: equity, a note, a loan or a revenue share. Terms are S13.

Say, don't print: your runway rule of thumb. Raising too little is worse than raising too much. Run out before the milestone and you raise again from weakness.

Predict before the click: "What kind of money fits this ask?" Answer: equipment financing, a bank line for seasonal working capital, or revenue share. Callback to slide 4: no fund-sized outcome, so a VC passes.

The lesson for this room: most of you should be pitching lenders, partners and customers, not VCs. Protect this point even if you're short on time.

Test 6 needs believable milestones and a credible path to a return. How investors think about that is S12.

Part 6 · In the room

Winning Pitch Tactics

Before
  • Enlist shared network outreach
  • Plant conversation starters
  • Match the detail to what they know
In the room
  • Invite pushback"Tell me more…"
  • Ask what you're missing"What am I missing?"
  • Admit what you don't know"I'll get back to you tomorrow."
  • Read their interest level
After
  • Send thank-you cards
  • Ask who else you should talk to
  • Ask permission to send updates
Fitler MBA · S11 · Part 6

Winning pitch tactics

Shared network outreach: a warm intro from someone the investor trusts beats any cold email. Find who you both know.

Conversation starters are deliberate hooks in the deck. They invite the question you want to answer.

Ask early: "How familiar are you with this space?" Then pitch to what they know.

"I'll get back to you tomorrow" only works if you do it. The follow-up is the second pitch.

A handwritten thank-you card stands out because almost nobody sends one.

"Who else should I talk to?" turns a no into an intro.

Part 6 · In the room

Pitch Killers

Before
  • Pitch before you've talked to customers
  • Email the deck you present
  • Ask for an NDA
In the room
  • Bury them in detail
  • Inflate the numbers
  • Claim you have no competition
  • Duck the "why you" question
  • Talk the whole time
  • Leave without a clear ask
After
  • Skip the thank-you note
  • Skip the follow-up
  • Follow up too much
  • Go silent on status updates
Fitler MBA · S11 · Part 6

Pitch killers

Beat: "Which of these have you done?" Show of hands. Thirty seconds.

Story slot: your worst pitch meeting.

Most VCs won't sign NDAs. Angels sometimes do. Asking marks you as new.

"No competition" means no market, or you haven't looked.

The deck you present is sparse because you're talking. Read cold, it falls flat and you never hear why. Send a read-ahead that stands on its own.

Follow-up: too little and you're forgotten, too much and you're a pest. Regular status updates are the middle path. They show progress without asking for anything.

Number your pages. They need to say "go back to slide 7." And be on time.
